newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac statement falls flat in French markets.
newsitem.headline: Chirac statement falls flat in French markets.

text.p: A statement by President Jacques Chirac on Tuesday had little effect on French financial markets and was not likely to boost the centre-right coalition's chances of victory Sunday's second round of a parliamentary election, analysts said.

They said the speech, almost certainly Chirac's last chance to influence the outcome of the vote, changed little since the president had stuck with his current policies in pursuit of a single European currency.
The franc along with debt and interest rate futures were barely moved by the short television speech, in which Chirac warned the French from returning to Socialism.

"All of it is pretty much going over the same ground," said Iain Lindsay, senior bond analyst at Credit Lyonnais. "I don't see this as a decisive issue for the RPR and the UDF," he said, referring to France's main centre right parties.

The president called for a modern, decentralised government reconciling economic freedom with social solidarity and gave no hint of which conservative politician he would choose to succeed Prime Minister Alain Juppe if the right won the runoff.

"I hope the majority which you will choose does not take the risk of weakening European integration," he said, after pledging tax cuts to quicken growth and overcome France's record 12.8 percent unemployment.
Lindsay said Chirac's speech made clear he intended to continue the broad lines of his economic policies aimed at boosting the economy with more labour market freedom and lower charges.
A futures trader in Paris said June PIBOR dipped slightly after the statement but the effect was short lived.

"PIBOR dipped a little, people were waiting for a name," the trader said, referring to rumours that Chirac would name a successor to Juppe, who pledged on Monday to step down regardless of the election's outcome.

Paul Horne, senior economist with Smith Barney in Paris, said Chirac appeared resigned to sharing power with Socialist leader Lionel Jospin, who would become prime minister if the combined left won the election.
"He seemed to be preparing the way for a cohabitation," Horne said.
June PIBOR was at 96.27 in afterhours trading, off three basis points from its close on Tuesday. The June bond future was unchanged at 128.44.

The franc was trading at 3.3772 per mark, roughly where it stood after National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin, a leading contender to replace Juppe, called earlier on Tuesday for a looser approach to Europe's planned single currency.
